paragraphs: Thutmose III's own officers argued against the direct route to Megiddo, a track through the Aruna pass so narrow that soldiers had to march single file with the horses trailing behind, warning that an ambush there could cut the army apart. He took it anyway, and found the enemy coalition had massed at the pass's two easier exits, leaving the direct road undefended.

After the rout, Egyptian troops stopped to strip the abandoned camp of chariots and armour instead of chasing survivors through Megiddo's open gates. The delay let the gates close, and Thutmose walled the city in with a moat and a timber palisade, starving it out over seven months. A scribe named Tjaneni kept the field notes, later carved onto the walls at Karnak, that let historians reconstruct the campaign day by day.

Eight British soldiers fired into a crowd on King Street on the night of 5 March 1770, after townspeople pelted them with snowballs, ice and oyster shells. A musket was knocked from one soldier's hand, a shot went off, and the rest of the line fired without a clear order. Crispus Attucks, an escaped slave working as a dockworker and sailor, was among the first to fall.

Within weeks, silversmith Paul Revere issued an engraving of the shooting copied almost line for line from a drawing by Henry Pelham, and sold it before Pelham's own reached print, crediting no one. That December, John Adams, later a president, defended the soldiers and won acquittals for six of them; the other two were convicted of manslaughter and branded on the thumb instead of hanged.

On 13 April 1919, Brigadier General Reginald Dyer marched about fifty riflemen to the single exit of Jallianwala Bagh, a walled garden in Amritsar where thousands had gathered for a spring festival and a banned political meeting. He ordered them to fire into the crowd without warning and kept them firing for roughly ten minutes, stopping only when ammunition ran low.

The Hunter Commission that investigated set the toll at 379 dead; a Congress inquiry that Gandhi helped organise counted nearly 1,200. Dyer told the commission he had fired to, in his words, strike terror throughout Punjab. The Commons voted 247 to 37 to condemn him in 1920; the Lords voted 129 to 86 to back him instead.
